[PATH:empirical] Borjas, G. J. (2003). The labor demand curve is downward sloping: Reexamining the impact of immigration on the labor market. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 118(4), 1335-1374. — This foundational study uses a spatial correlations approach across U.S. local labor markets, providing direct empirical evidence on how immigration affects wages and employment of native workers with low education, especially during economic downturns. Replicating its analysis with data from 2008-2009 recession and focusing on low-skill-overlap areas could confirm or refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Card, D., & DiNardo, J. (2000). Do immigrant inflows lead to native outflows? American Economic Review, 90(2), 360-367. — This paper examines the relationship between immigrant inflows and native internal migration, which is crucial for understanding job displacement risk. Extending its analysis to periods of recession and to local markets with low skill overlap would test whether displacement effects are magnified under those conditions.

[PATH:theoretical] Dustmann, C., Schönberg, U., & Stuhler, J. (2017). Labor supply shocks, native wages, and the adjustment of local labor markets. Journal of Labor Economics, 35(1), 1-41. — This paper develops a theoretical framework distinguishing between short-run and long-run labor market adjustments to immigration, incorporating skill overlap and business cycle effects. Applying this model to simulate wage dispersion and displacement risk for low-education natives during downturns would provide a rigorous theoretical test of the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Card, D. (1990). 'The Impact of the Mariel Boatlift on the Miami Labor Market.' Industrial and Labor Relations Review, 43(2), 245-257. — This seminal natural experiment study provides direct empirical evidence on how a sudden influx of low-skilled immigrants affected native wages in a local labor market, offering a baseline to test the hypothesis that immigration increases native wages through productivity effects.

[PATH:empirical] Peri, G. (2012). 'The Effect of Immigration on Productivity: Evidence from U.S. States.' Review of Economics and Statistics, 94(1), 348-358. — This study explicitly examines the link between immigration-induced labor supply shifts and productivity gains at the state level, providing empirical evidence on the productivity channel hypothesized to raise native wages.

[PATH:theoretical] Borjas, G.J. (2003). 'The Labor Demand Curve Is Downward Sloping: Reexamining the Impact of Immigration on the Labor Market.' Quarterly Journal of Economics, 118(4), 1335-1374. — This paper presents a competing theoretical framework predicting negative wage effects for native workers in local labor markets, offering a critical counterpoint to the hypothesis and guiding further empirical tests to resolve the dispute.

[PATH:literature] National Bureau of Economic Research Working Paper Series, 'Immigration and the Labor Market: A Meta-Analysis' (e.g., Longhi et al., 2005 or updated versions) — A meta-analysis summarizing effect sizes across many studies can reveal whether the wage effect for native workers consistently depends on local skill composition, helping to validate or refute the conditional claim.

[PATH:theoretical] American Economic Review, 'The Labor Market Effects of Immigration: A Structural Approach' (e.g., Borjas, 2003 or later structural models) — A structural model of labor demand and supply with skill heterogeneity can simulate wage outcomes under varying native education shares, providing a theoretical benchmark to assess the plausibility of the 30% threshold.

[PATH:empirical] Borjas, G. J. (2003). 'The Labor Demand Curve Is Downward Sloping: Reexamining the Impact of Immigration on the Labor Market.' Quarterly Journal of Economics, 118(4), 1335-1374. — This seminal paper uses a national-level approach to estimate the effect of immigration on native wages, finding negative effects for low-skill workers. Replicating its methodology on high-skill native workers in urban markets post-1980 could test whether skill complementarity mitigates or reverses the wage effect.

[PATH:empirical] Card, D. (2001). 'Immigrant Inflows, Native Outflows, and the Local Labor Market Impact of Higher Immigration.' Journal of Labor Economics, 19(1), 22-64. — Card's spatial correlation approach examines local labor market impacts of immigration, including wage effects on native workers. Extending this analysis to high-skill complementarity contexts (e.g., tech hubs) could provide direct evidence on whether wage decreases occur specifically in such markets.

[PATH:theoretical] Ottaviano, G. I. P., & Peri, G. (2012). 'Rethinking the Effect of Immigration on Wages.' Journal of the European Economic Association, 10(1), 152-197. — This paper develops a theoretical model distinguishing between perfect and imperfect substitution of immigrant and native labor. Applying its framework to high-skill complementarity scenarios would clarify whether wage decreases are theoretically plausible or offset by productivity gains.

Replicating or updating this analysis for 1990-2020 can confirm or refute the hypothesized negative effect.

[PATH:empirical] Card, D. (1990). 'The Impact of the Mariel Boatlift on the Miami Labor Market.' Industrial and Labor Relations Review, 43(2), 245-257. — This natural experiment study examines a sudden influx of immigrants into Miami and finds minimal effects on native wages. It serves as a key counterexample to the hypothesis, and re-analyzing its data with updated methods or extending the temporal scope to 2020 can test the robustness of the null result.

[PATH:theoretical] Ottaviano, G.I.P., & Peri, G. (2012). 'Rethinking the Effect of Immigration on Wages.' Journal of the European Economic Association, 10(1), 152-197. — This paper develops a general equilibrium model that distinguishes between imperfect substitution of immigrant and native labor, showing that immigration can raise native wages in the long run. Applying its framework to local labor market data for 1990-2020 would provide theoretical grounding to evaluate whether the hypothesized direct competition effect is offset by complementarities.
